strengths: Introduction of a novel and substantial dataset domain: spatial multigraphs with rich, continuous geometric edge trajectories, bridging non-Hermitian quantum physics / band theory and geometric graph representation learning.

Impressive scale and efficiency: The Poly2Graph pipeline leverages companion matrix formulations, parallel eigensolvers, and adaptive image-thinning techniques to achieve substantial computational speedups and memory efficiency, enabling the generation of 11.6M static and 5.1M dynamic graphs across 1,401 classes.

Thorough open-source tooling and documentation: Poly2Graph is provided with extensive examples, API documentation, and tutorials in the appendix, offering practical utility for both condensed matter researchers and machine learning practitioners.
Clear analysis of the dataset properties, including class distribution, non-isomorphic topological variants (HSG-topology), and temporal parameter trajectories (T-HSG-5M).
weaknesses: Limited baseline selection: Although the dataset explicitly emphasizes spatial multigraph structures, the empirical evaluation is limited to four standard simple-graph GNNs (GCN, GIN, GAT, GraphSAGE). The paper lacks comparisons against existing multigraph GNNs (e.g., Egressy et al., 2024; Butler et al., 2023) or continuous geometric/spatial graph architectures (e.g., DimeNet, EGNN, or trajectory-based encoders).

Under-trained benchmarking setup: Models are trained for only 5 epochs on a single GPU without early stopping or systematic hyperparameter search, raising questions about whether the reported performance differences stem from underfitting rather than fundamental representational bottlenecks.

Data extraction artifacts: As acknowledged in Section B.5, the morphological skeletonization approach suffers from 'component fragmentation' in low-DOS regimes, which may introduce spurious topological disconnections that distort the true spectrum topology.

Overstated universality claims regarding general linear algebra: The claim in Section 6 and Appendix E that spectral graphs act as universal topological fingerprints for arbitrary matrices relies on non-unique Toeplitz decompositions and is not demonstrated or benchmarked on any concrete downstream linear algebra tasks.

strengths: Novel and unique graph domain: The dataset focuses on spatial multigraphs with rich, non-linear edge geometry derived from 1D crystal Hamiltonians in non-Hermitian quantum physics, filling a notable void in standard graph representation learning benchmarks.

Substantial scale and generative pipeline: The paper introduces a massive collection (11.6M static and 5.1M temporal graphs across 1401 classes) and provides Poly2Graph, a highly optimized, GPU-accelerated, open-source pipeline utilizing Frobenius companion matrix solvers and adaptive image skeletonization.

Comprehensive mathematical grounding and documentation: The appendices provide rigorous background on non-Bloch band theory, the electrostatic analogy, Generalized Brillouin Zones, and a detailed tutorial for utilizing the Python library.
weaknesses: Preliminary and limited machine learning benchmarking: Evaluation is restricted to four basic standard GNNs (GCN, GIN, GAT, GraphSAGE) trained for only 5 epochs on small-to-medium subsets. The flagship 11.6M dataset (HSG-12M) and the dynamic collection (T-HSG-5M) have zero experimental results.

Absence of domain-appropriate baselines: Despite emphasizing that the key challenge is learning on spatial multigraphs with rich edge geometry and temporal sequences, the benchmark does not include any multigraph-specific architectures (e.g., Egressy et al., 2024), geometric/continuous-edge GNNs, or spatio-temporal graph models.

Data extraction artifacts and topological noise: As acknowledged in Section 6 and Appendix B.5, the pipeline suffers from 'component fragmentation' in regimes with low density of states (DOS), introducing spurious disconnections and artifacts into the extracted graph topologies.

Task formulation and data leakage concerns: Graphs within each class are generated by sweeping two continuous parameters (a, b) over a regular grid. Standard random or stratified splitting across all graphs risks substantial data leakage between train and test distributions; evaluating out-of-distribution or parameter-extrapolation splits would be much more indicative of actual model capability.

strengths: Scale and Data Modality: Introduces a very large dataset (11.6M static and 5.1M temporal graphs) focusing on spatial multigraphs with rich, non-linear edge geometries, filling a recognized void in graph benchmarks where multi-edges and spatial trajectories are typically collapsed.

Open-Source Pipeline: The Poly2Graph extraction pipeline is clearly explained and significantly speeds up spectral potential computation and root-finding (via companion matrix eigensolving and GPU acceleration), providing an accessible tool for researchers in this domain.

Interdisciplinary Connection: The work establishes an interesting connection between non-Hermitian quantum band theory, algebraic geometry (Laurent characteristic polynomials), and graph representation learning.
Detailed Documentation: The appendix provides comprehensive background on non-Bloch band theory, extensive data schema descriptions, and code tutorials for the package.
weaknesses: Weak and Incomplete Benchmarks: The experimental evaluation is quite preliminary. Only standard, off-the-shelf GNN baselines (GCN, GIN, GAT, GraphSAGE) are evaluated, none of which natively account for multigraph structure or continuous spatial edge geometries. Furthermore, models were only trained for 5 epochs on smaller subsets; no experiments are provided on the main HSG-12M dataset or the dynamic T-HSG-5M benchmark.

Synthetic Task Formulation and Practical Utility: The primary task is classifying the underlying polynomial class from the extracted spectral graph. Because both the graphs and the labels are generated synthetically from polynomial specifications, it functions as an artificial inverse problem. The real-world utility and direct physics value of this specific classification task remain tenuous compared to standard scientific ML benchmarks.

Pipeline Artifacts and Component Fragmentation: The image-based extraction pipeline (binarizing 2D DOS landscapes followed by morphological thinning) suffers from 'component fragmentation' in regimes with low density of states or high hopping ranges. This introduces heuristic topological errors and spurious disconnections into the benchmark data.

Overstated Claims on Universality: The claim that spectral graphs serve as a 'universal topological fingerprint' for arbitrary matrices relies on Toeplitz decomposition, which is highly non-unique and arbitrary, making its utility as a canonical graph representation in general linear algebra questionable.

strengths: Novel and under-explored graph modality: HSG-12M provides the first large-scale benchmark of spatial multigraphs, where multiple geometrically distinct edges between node pairs are preserved rather than collapsed, filling an important gap in graph representation learning benchmarks.

Efficient end-to-end extraction pipeline: Poly2Graph leverages companion matrix eigensolving and a two-stage adaptive resolution scheme to achieve up to 10^5x speedup over prior manual/semi-automated procedures, enabling the practical construction of a 12M-graph dataset.

Solid theoretical and interdisciplinary grounding: The dataset is firmly rooted in non-Bloch band theory and non-Hermitian quantum physics, while also establishing an intriguing algebraic connection via Toeplitz decomposition of general matrices.

Thorough benchmark design and controlled evaluation: The authors benchmark eight representative GNN architectures across multiple subsets with carefully matched parameter budgets, demonstrating that incorporating spatial multi-edge features significantly improves performance over edge-agnostic counterparts.
weaknesses: Information bottleneck in benchmark featurization: Although the raw dataset preserves complete continuous edge trajectories as ordered coordinate sequences, the benchmark experiments reduce these rich curves to fixed 6-dimensional summary statistics (midpoint, length, straight-line distance, average DOS/potential), partially blunting the distinctiveness of the continuous spatial multigraph modality in the empirical evaluation.

Absence of dedicated spatial multigraph architectures: The experimental study exclusively evaluates standard off-the-shelf GNN baselines rather than introducing or adapting models explicitly designed for continuous curve geometries or dense multi-edge interactions.

Artifacts from image-based extraction: As acknowledged in the limitations, the pipeline relies on global thresholding and morphological thinning of the density-of-states landscape, which can suffer from 'component fragmentation' (spurious topological disconnections) in regions with low spectral density.

Synthetic nature of the inverse design task: While classifying characteristic polynomial classes from spectral graphs is physically motivated as a candidate retrieval step, the sampling scheme over polynomial coefficients is synthetic, and no downstream physical simulation or experimental validation of candidate retrieval is demonstrated.

strengths: Novel and under-served graph modality: Introduces the first large-scale benchmark specifically dedicated to spatial multigraphs with non-trivial continuous edge geometry, addressing a significant blind spot in graph representation learning benchmarks where edges are almost universally simple or collapsed into single scalar attributes.

Massive scale and diversity: HSG-12M contains 11.6 million static and 5.1 million dynamic graphs spanning 1,401 classes, making it one of the largest graph-level classification datasets available in the natural sciences.

High-performance extraction pipeline: Poly2Graph cleverly combines algebraic companion-matrix root finding, non-Bloch band theory, and adaptive two-stage morphological processing to achieve up to 5 orders of magnitude speedup over prior unautomated methods.

Rigorous grounding in physical theory: The dataset is firmly rooted in non-Hermitian condensed matter physics (generalized Brillouin zone, Ronkin functions, and density of states), opening up promising avenues for AI-driven inverse material design and algebraic topology exploration.

Thorough evaluation and documentation: The paper provides extensive mathematical background, comparison with 45 existing graph datasets, a detailed API tutorial, and well-controlled benchmark experiments equalizing parameter budgets across eight standard GNN architectures.
weaknesses: Simplification in benchmarking featurization: While the raw dataset stores full polyline coordinate sequences for edges, the benchmark baseline converts them into fixed-size summary statistics (length, midpoint, straight-line distance, mean potential/DOS). The paper does not evaluate any specialized model directly processing continuous edge polylines or curves.

Absence of specialized multigraph or geometric GNN baselines: The evaluated models are restricted to standard, general-purpose GNNs (GCN, GAT, GIN, GraphSAGE, etc.). Including specialized multigraph GNN architectures (such as those cited in Section A.2) or recent graph Transformers would provide stronger and more modern benchmark points.

Vulnerability to component fragmentation: As noted in the limitations, the morphological skeletonization can suffer from numerical artifacts (component fragmentation) in regions of low density of states, potentially introducing topological noise into the ground-truth graphs for more complex band structures.

strengths: Ambitious scale and novel physical domain: The paper introduces HSG-12M, containing 11.6M static and 5.1M dynamic graphs across 1,401 classes derived from non-Bloch band theory in non-Hermitian quantum systems, representing an enormous effort in data synthesis.

Well-engineered extraction pipeline: Poly2Graph provides an automated, GPU-accelerated pipeline combining companion matrix eigensolving, Ronkin potential calculation, and adaptive computer vision techniques to convert Laurent polynomials to spatial multigraphs with significant speedups over prior manual/semi-manual approaches.

Rich structural representations: Unlike standard graph benchmarks that discard multi-edges or restrict edges to abstract pairwise connections, the dataset stores ordered sequences of spatial coordinates along edge curves, preserving geometric trajectories in the complex energy plane.

Thorough documentation and open-source release: The manuscript includes extensive background material, pipeline pseudo-code, code tutorials, and comparative tables against 45 existing graph benchmarks.
weaknesses: Disconnect between dataset representation and benchmark execution: Although the central motivation of the paper is the preservation of continuous spatial multi-edge geometry, the benchmarking framework collapses these rich edge curves into a simplistic 6-dimensional summary vector (straight-line distance, midpoint coordinates, length, and average scalar fields). Consequently, the experiments do not evaluate architectures capable of learning over continuous geometric trajectories, undermining the core methodological motivation.

Omission of multigraph and spatial GNN baselines: The benchmark only evaluates standard simple-graph GNN architectures (GCN, GAT, GIN, GraphSAGE, etc.). Despite citing dedicated multigraph learning methods (e.g., Butler et al., 2023; Egressy et al., 2024) and spatial graph models, none are benchmarked to demonstrate how multigraph-specific inductive biases handle this dataset.

Complete absence of benchmarks for the dynamic dataset: While the generation of 5.1M temporal graphs (T-HSG-5M) is emphasized as a primary contribution in the abstract and introduction, the paper provides zero experimental evaluation, baseline results, or formal benchmark task definitions for dynamic/temporal graph learning.

Synthetic task framing and questionable utility for true inverse design: The classification task consists of identifying the underlying Laurent monomial support (ChP class) from graphs generated by varying only two coefficients on a regular grid. Real-world materials and physical experimental data feature disorder, noise, and open parameter spaces; claiming that 1401-way discrete classification of synthetic polynomials operationalizes practical inverse design without experimental validation or parameter regression is an overstatement.

Heuristic extraction artifacts ('Component Fragmentation'): As acknowledged in Appendix C.6 and shown in Figure A4, the computer vision skeletonization pipeline suffers from numerical instability and threshold sensitivity when the density of states is low, leading to spurious disconnections and component fragmentation in the extracted ground truth graphs.
